comparison: Both evaluate evolutionary speculation claims (C166-C184). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting claims are 'explicitly speculative' and 'remain plausible interpretations requiring future empirical validation.' Peer review also rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 finding speculations 'useful' but 'not convincing' initially, later noting they remain 'likely still to be controversial.' Both agree these are open questions rather than established conclusions.

Both address right monocular test in Experiment 2 (C132-C137). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to non-significant between-group comparison (BF=1.678) despite Li-chicks' within-group success, noting 'interpretation requires caution.' Peer review rates SUPPORTED, accepting this as part of overall behavioral evidence and hemispheric specialization framework. Peer reviewers do not explicitly discuss the statistical ambiguity that concerns OpenEval.

Both evaluate core directional bias findings from Experiment 1 (C12, C99-C105, C140-C142). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with strong statistical evidence (large effect sizes, BF=337.124 for Li-chicks' left bias). Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with all reviewers affirming this as 'compelling' evidence and the 'core finding.' Complete agreement on this central result.

Both address left monocular test failure in Experiment 2 (C127-C131). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting statistical evidence shows no group differences and interpreting this as right hemisphere reliance on spatial information. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, accepting this pattern as part of overall evidence without challenge. Both agree on the finding and its interpretation regarding right hemisphere limitations.

Both evaluate disappearance of directional bias in Experiment 2 (C11, C121-C125, C147). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on statistical evidence showing no bias in either group when spatial cues unreliable. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 acknowledging bias appeared only 'when the distance between items gave a reliable spatial cue.' Both agree this contrast with Experiment 1 is central to the study's logic.

Both address experimental methodology (C6-C9, C83-C95). OpenEval rates training/testing procedures as SUPPORTED, noting clear description and validation from previous studies. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 stating 'Behavioral evidence is strong enough' and Reviewer 2 praising 'Novel methodology.' Both accept the experimental design as sound.

OpenEval R1 addresses experimental manipulation and sample (C6-C7, C80-C82). Peer R11 addresses light exposure manipulation (C59-C68, C81-C82). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes manipulation is 'well-established in the literature.' Peer review confirms 'light-exposure induced lateralization' was 'critical for the successful analysis' and accepts it as valid. Both agree on the validity of the lateralization manipulation.

Both address left monocular test in Experiment 1 (C106-C110). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with very strong statistical evidence (BF=5598.452, d=2.088). Peer review also rates SUPPORTED as part of monocular findings that contribute to 'compelling' evidence. Both agree these results support the hemispheric contribution claims.

OpenEval R7 addresses right monocular test in Experiment 1 (C113-C116). Peer R3 includes these claims (C113-C116) along with other monocular findings. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites strong statistical evidence (BF=6887.511). Peer review accepts monocular results as supporting hemispheric contributions. Both agree on the validity of these findings.

OpenEval R16 synthesizes light stimulation effects (C186-C191). Peer R3 includes some overlapping claims about monocular performance. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes Li-chicks' success in monocular conditions suggesting right hemisphere dominance. Peer review accepts light-exposure lateralization as important for the findings. Both agree on the role of lateralization.

OpenEval R4 addresses sagittal test findings (C10, C96-C98, C185). Peer R1 includes C10, C98 among broader core findings. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes large effect size (d=0.904) and strong BF. Peer review accepts this as part of 'compelling' evidence for main conclusions. Both agree on the validity of these results.

OpenEval R14 synthesizes main conclusions (C13-C14, C111, C126, C142-C146). Peer R1 includes overlapping claims (C14, C142-C146) in core findings. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes 'convergent evidence across multiple tests.' Peer review describes evidence as 'compelling' with all reviewers affirming core findings. Complete agreement on main conclusions.

Both address main conclusions about lateralization and spatial-numerical associations (C13, C111, C126). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on convergent evidence. Peer R6 also rates SUPPORTED, with editor and reviewers affirming the study 'demonstrates how a left-right bias...depends on brain lateralization.' Both agree on the core theoretical conclusions.

Both address hemispheric specialization claims (C161-C163). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting right hemisphere evidence is stronger while left hemisphere evidence relies on non-significant between-group comparison. Peer R6 rates SUPPORTED, accepting hemispheric specialization framework without noting statistical limitations. Peer reviewers are more accepting of the hemispheric specialization interpretation than OpenEval.

Both evaluate theoretical model comparisons (C195-C196, C202-C205). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting experimental design tested model predictions and findings support right-hemisphere dominance model. Peer R13 also rates SUPPORTED, accepting theoretical framework as appropriate contextualization. Both agree the theoretical synthesis is well-grounded in the data.

OpenEval R8 synthesizes Experiment 1 findings (C117-C118, C138-C139). Peer R7 addresses performance advantage of lateralized brains (includes C117-C118). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes consistent pattern across tests. Peer review confirms authors 'are successful in revealing that the lateralized brain is advantageous.' Both agree on the synthesis of Experiment 1 results.

OpenEval R9 addresses sagittal test in Experiment 2 (C11, C119-C121). Peer R2 includes C11, C121 among claims about spatial cue dependence. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes very small effect size and BF favoring null. Peer review accepts this as part of the contrast between experiments. Both agree on the finding of no group difference.

OpenEval R13 synthesizes Experiment 2 key findings (C147-C148, C163, C176). Peer R2 includes C147 among claims about spatial cue dependence. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes disappearance of effects when spatial information unreliable. Peer review accepts this contrast as central to study logic. Both agree on the interpretation of Experiment 2 results.

OpenEval R3 addresses experimental manipulation distinguishing the two experiments (C90-C95). Peer R12 includes these claims in overall methodology evaluation. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes manipulation is 'clearly described and logically designed.' Peer review accepts methodology as sound. Both agree on the validity of the experimental design.

Peer R8 addresses framing around 'Mental Number Line' terminology and human numerical spatialization (C1-C4, C17-C24). Rated UNCERTAIN by peer reviewers, with Reviewer 2 extensively challenging the framing as 'highly contentious' and requesting terminology changes. No corresponding OpenEval result directly addresses these background/framing claims. Peer reviewers identified concerns about contextualization that OpenEval did not separately evaluate.

Peer R9 addresses claims about innateness versus developmental plasticity (C3-C4, C25-C30). Rated UNCERTAIN by peer reviewers, with Reviewer 2 questioning whether findings demonstrate innateness given that experimental manipulation matters. No corresponding OpenEval result directly addresses these conceptual claims about innateness. Peer reviewers raised theoretical concerns about the innate/developmental distinction that OpenEval did not separately evaluate.

Peer R10 addresses novelty claims about being first to test lateralization's role (C5, C41, C52-C54). Rated SUPPORTED by peer reviewers who acknowledge this as 'the first study' with 'Novel methodology.' No corresponding OpenEval result directly addresses these novelty/contribution claims. Peer reviewers explicitly evaluated the study's novel contribution, which OpenEval did not separately assess.
